claims.text: S8 demonstrates that architectural interventions—specifically models that grow depth during training—achieve substantially different compute-optimal allocations than vanilla transformers. A 7.4B parameter model grown during training matches GPT-3 (13B) on the CORE benchmark while using less total compute, showing that the scaling exponent itself changes with architecture choice, not merely the efficiency constant.

claims.text: S9 documents that Kaplan (2020) and Chinchilla (2022) prescribed different optimal allocations—Kaplan favored greater parameter growth while Chinchilla favored equal parameter and token scaling. However, much of this divergence stems from different accounting conventions: Kaplan used non-embedding parameters while Chinchilla used total parameters. Since embedding parameters represent a larger fraction of smaller models, this counting difference significantly affects the fitted scaling exponents when applied to different model-size ranges.

claims.text: The Chinchilla scaling laws (Hoffmann et al., March 2022) measured performance divergence empirically across over 400 models (70M to 16B parameters). At identical training compute, a 70-billion-parameter model trained on 1.4 trillion tokens outperformed a 280-billion-parameter model with fewer tokens (Gopher), achieving 67.5% on MMLU—greater than 7% improvement—while enabling cheaper inference. This established that compute-optimal allocation is approximately 20 tokens per parameter, and misaligned ratios produce systematically worse end-state performance.

claims.text: Whether misaligned parameter-to-token allocations matter forever depends on the mathematical form of your success metric. For bounded metrics (validation accuracy capped at 100%, code correctness as pass/fail), smaller models trained longer eventually match frontier models despite exponential divergence in compute investment. For unbounded metrics (reasoning depth, task length), frontier models maintain permanent advantages. This means capability domains will bifurcate: some see meek models inherit capability access while others see concentration persist indefinitely.

claims.text: Modern frontier and open-weight models intentionally misalign beyond compute-optimal allocation for inference economics. Llama-3 8B was trained on 15 trillion tokens at 8 billion parameters (1,875 tokens/parameter), approximately two orders of magnitude higher than Chinchilla's 20 tokens/parameter compute-optimal rate. This reversal from compute-optimal allocation accepts higher training costs because inference cost dominates total lifetime cost once deployed at scale.
